column4: Expanding the Food and Nutrition Research Institute's  Nutrigenomics Laboratory: Towards Establishment of a World-Class Philippine Center for Nutritional Genomics
column6:
Recent advances in molecular biology and the wealth of information generated by the Human Genome Project have paved the way for a new era in nutritional research—Nutrigenomics. In its early stages, research at the Food and Nutrition Research Institute (FNRI) focused on understanding the genetic basis of nutrition and health outcomes. Today, it has evolved into a comprehensive nutrition omics program, encompassing not only genomics but also metagenomics, metabolomics, DNA barcoding, and imminently, other emerging omics technologies.

This strategic expansion aims to foster molecular-based elucidation of nutrition and health outcomes in the Filipino population. By integrating multi-omics platforms with data from the National Nutrition Survey (NNS), the ongoing Eastern Visayas Birth Cohort, and other collaborative projects, FNRI’s nutrition omics research provides a holistic understanding of the complex interactions between genetics, microbiome composition, metabolic profiles, and dietary patterns. This systems biology approach allows for a deeper investigation into how nutrition influences health at the molecular level, enabling the development of precision nutrition strategies tailored to the genetic makeup, gut microbiome, and metabolic characteristics of specific Filipino subpopulations.

The integration of genomics, metagenomics, and metabolomics into nutrition research opens new avenues for understanding the nutrient-gene-microbiome interactions that contribute to non-communicable diseases, obesity, stunting, and other public health concerns. This initiative is particularly crucial during critical life stages, such as the first 1000 days of life, immunocompromised states, and older age, where nutrition plays a pivotal role in immune function and overall health.

Aligned with the government’s thrust on universal health care and its commitment to inclusive growth, this project advances nutrition omics research to bridge health gaps and contribute to evidence-based public health policies. By integrating multi-omics data with nutrition phenotypes, FNRI can generate insights into the social, cultural, economic, and dietary determinants of non-communicable diseases and micronutrient deficiencies, paving the way for targeted dietary interventions and healthful food products specifically designed for Filipinos.

The DOST-FNRI's vision for Nutrigenomics is that the Philippines shall be recognized as a highly competent and competitive research body in terms of Nutrigenomics R&D with a sophisticated and world-class Nutrigenomics Center that provides services both locally and internationally. The complexity of interactions among genes, nutritional and functional food components, and lifestyle will be a great challenge to solve. Strategies will include the essential requisite to upgrade the nutrigenomics laboratory in the country to cater to the needs of the researchers, the need for new competencies in the conduct of research and the application of nutrigenomics, and finally collaboration with other research entities whose research align with the main thrusts of nutrigenomics. The expanded nutritional genomics Laboratory will focus on the following areas: 1) role of nutrients on gene expression; 2) the impact of dietary signals in the genome; 3) polymorphism detection (for molecular epidemiology research; 4) genome health and stability as mediated by nutrition.

column4: Construction of Saliksik Extension Building (Proposed PCHRD Green Building Extension-formerly Modernization of Saliksik Building)
column5: Philippine Council for Health Research and Development
column6:
Currently, PCHRD is housed in Saliksik Building, occupying a floor area of approximately 470 square meters. Having one hundred eighty-six (186) employees as of December 31, 2023, the estimated employee-to-floor area ratio is 1:2.53 square meters exclusive of storage area requirements.

From 2004-2023, PCHRD’s budget increased by approximately 1,937.47%. Add to that the substantial amount of funds from other Institutions (e.g. DOH) being managed by PCHRD (which continues to increase every year), it is a given that the number of projects and personnel managing the projects will increase. Currently PCHRD has around 160 employees trying to fit in a small space. 

More projects also mean more paper files as required by our ISO certification and by the National Archives of the Philippines. Thus, we will also need more storage spaces. 

The proposed extension building will address the shortage of space for the increasing number of PCHRD personnel, as well as space for other amenities like a conference room and storage rooms for documents. 

Aside from organic PCHRD staff, the proposed building will also house the Philippine National Health Research System (PNHRS) - related committee secretariats, as well as the Philippine Health Research Ethics Board (PHREB), National Ethics Committee (NEC), and COA office. It will also house the ASEAN-NDI Secretariat, the DOH Program staff, and other special projects staff. 

Upon completion of the design revision, an increase in the total estimated amount shall be observed due to the following reasons: a.) Inflation of materials within three (3) years from the original DAED; b.) New top soil volume that will affect the earthwork and structural works; c.) new labor cost; and d.) area extension of the site.

For FY 2024, there is an insertion fund in the amount of PhP 30,000,000.00 which will be utilized mainly on the General Requirements, Permits and Clearances, Clearing and Preparation of Site, Excavation and Hauling, and Foundation Works.
The Total Project Cost for the Construction of the Saliksik Extension Building (Phase 2) is Php 937.7 Million. This amount includes the Approved Budget for the Contract, which totaled Php 884.5 Million, plus an additional six percent for Construction Project Management (CPM). Furthermore, the 30 Million CICA is on top of the total project cost estimates for the Construction of Saliksik Building Extension Building.

column4: Construction of Agricultural Technology, Enterprise & Resource Center (ATERC)
column6:
The proposed Agricultural Technology, Enterprise & Resource Center (ATERC) is a strategic and essential initiative by Pampanga State Agricultural University (PSAU) designed to serve as the primary nexus for agricultural technology transfer, commercialization, and sustainable livelihood enterprise development in Central Luzon. The rationale for investment is clear: a significant and persistent gap exists between valuable agricultural research and its successful translation into viable, income-generating businesses for rural communities. The ATERC complex will resolve this by functioning as a dynamic repository and showcase, exhibiting a curated selection of proven, market-ready farm technologies along with their complete financial and resource requirements. This provides a tangible platform for businessmen, potential agri-entrepreneurs, and agricultural workers to explore viable projects for themselves and their families. By offering pre-vetted technologies and accompanying business models, the ATERC will guide interested visitors in finding workable agribusiness ideas and accessing the necessary resources for successful implementation, thereby moving PSAU's innovations directly into the regional economy.

This project is a crucial mechanism for generating significant rural employment and accelerating economic growth. It directly aligns with the Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023-2028 priority on food security and the creation of sustainable rural livelihoods. The impact is profound: the ATERC fulfills global commitments by supporting SDG 2 (Zero Hunger) through increased productivity and promoting sustainable agriculture, and SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) by fostering entrepreneurship and decent job creation in the vital rural sector. Investing in the ATERC is therefore a direct investment in the self-sufficiency and economic resilience of Filipino farming communities.

column4: Standards, Testing and Regulation for Industry Development and Enhanced Consumer Protection “Project STRIDE 3.0”
column6:
As the country moves toward economic recovery from the wrath of COVID-19 pandemic, it is evident more than ever that technical infrastructure and critical services that aid industry development, infuse economic activities and ensures maximum consumer protection must be taken. Along this line, the Bureau of Philippine Standards (BPS) is proposing the continuation of Project STRIDE - “Standards, Testing, and Regulation for Industry Development and Enhanced Consumer Protection” which aims to raise the competitiveness of products in the Philippine market and protect consumers through product quality and safety.
 
The BPS is committed to raising the quality and competitiveness of Philippine products and services, ensuring consumer safety and promoting environmental protection, contributing to the improvement of an enabling ecosystem for Philippine business, instilling standards, safety, and quality consciousness among Filipino people, and providing quality service to its clientele pursuant to its mandate under Republic Act 4109.
 
This proposal, Project STRIDE 3.0, aims to sustain the BPS’ commitment by expanding its services to cover more products that are critical to safeguarding consumer safety with the support of up-to-date and state-of-the-art testing facilities as described in the applicable Philippine National Standard (PNS). Also, with the facilitation of international trade, it is important to ensure that imported products are tested for their quality and safety prior to sale for the protection of the consuming public. Moreover, it aims to strengthen its testing capability to provide testing services to the local businesses.
 
The establishment of new testing facilities with up-to-date testing equipment will greatly support the BPS Mandatory Product Certification Schemes namely, (1) Philippine Standard (PS) Safety and/or Quality Certification Mark License and (2) Import Commodity Clearance (ICC) Certification, the main objective of which is to protect the public from substandard products and the inherent dangers and hazards while instilling quality consciousness to importers and manufacturers. This will also support the standards development process of the Bureau wherein the facilities can be used to vet the parameters set in the standards being developed, provide training facilities for upskilling of technical manpower particularly in the construction industry and conduct confirmatory test if there are any conflict on the result of private or government laboratory.

column4: Establishment of National Metrology Training Center of the Philippines
column6:
Metrology plays a vital yet seemingly imperceptible role in the economy – there is a defined measurement for every goods made, sold and bought. It lays down the foundation in the verification of goods and services, boosting the consumer and seller confidence. In the medical field, preliminary examination with the aid of medical devices is very important in the issuance of diagnosis to the patients. Advanced economies have already established their legal metrology system with a defined inspector certification program, supporting the implementation of their laws similar to our consumer code. 
Executive Order No. 128 mandates the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) to “provide central direction, leadership and coordination of scientific and technological efforts and ensure that the results therefrom are geared and utilized in areas of maximum economic and social benefits for the people”. The National Metrology Laboratory (NML) of the Industrial Technology Development Institute (ITDI), as the laboratory arm of the National Metrology Board (NMB) wherein the DOST Secretary is the Chair as stated in the Metrology Act of 2003, carrying out the functions of a National Metrology Institute for the country, it is incumbent for the NML to spearhead the establishment of the legal metrology system in the Philippines. One of the underpinning activities is strengthening the capabilities of the local legal metrology authorities, making sure that it is in alignment with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) requirements and International Organization for Legal Metrology (OIML) recommendations through the establishment of National Metrology Training Center of the Philippines.

column4: Innovating Nuclear Medicine Research and Services: Development of Emerging PET Radiopharmaceuticals for Early Cancer Staging and Assessment of Biologic Functions in Cancer Cells
column6:
Cancer is one of the top non communicable killer diseases in the Philippines, with a mortality rate of 60%. Out of approximately 100,000 diagnosed cases, about 60, 000 die annually due to the late diagnosis. According to the data available, between 2018 to 2040, it is predicted that the number of cancer incidence will increase by 69.4% for the male population, 56.8% for the female population. In terms of mortality, the estimated number of deaths is expected to increase by 74.5% for the male population and 67.7% for the female population.

Nuclear medicine technologies, such as hybrid imaging, using positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) techniques have been proven to be integral in the diagnostic algorithm in oncology, for example, in cancer staging and re-staging, specifically in lung, gastrointestinal, breast, malignant melanoma, head and neck, and other cancers. PET-CT scans using 18-F FDG are based on the uncontrolled metabolism of ‘glucose’ by cancer cells. Using a cyclotron, scientists have targeted the oxygen component of the glucose, converting this into radioactive fluorine (18F or FDG) which emits positrons for only a few hours. The radiopharmaceutical FDG is injected into the cancer patient, and the breakthrough in the imaging of the position radiation within the cancer cells with preferential uptake of the FGD allows a PET-CT SCAN determine the stage of the cancer illness. Although FDG PET and PET/CT have a well-established role in the management of most cancer patients, they also have some limitations with respect to specificity for certain types of cancer. For the last 15-20 years, a growing number of non-FDG PET tracers have been used in clinical research. Many of these new PET tracers are being investigated for the non-invasive assessment of different biologic functions in cancer cells such as detection of bone metastasis, prostate cancer detection, tumour cell receptor binding, proliferation, angiogenesis and hypnoxia imaging. More recently, researches have also indicated the use of PET Scans in Covid-19 related pulmonary infections and inflammations. 

To be able to have a tangible contributions for the advancement in health care, particularly in cancer diagnosis and management, the PNRI envision to position itself as a center of nuclear medicine research and development in Asia through innovations in radiopharmaceuticals for positron emission tomography applications, among others.

First and foremost will be the establishment of a 18-20 MeV radioisotope source in its primary facility and allied radiochemistry facilities.

column4: Strengthening Research, Instruction, Extension, and Innovation for Climate-Resilient Disease Prevention and Regional Health Security through Advanced Biotechnology Laboratory Systems at the Eastern Visayas Innovation Center for Health Biotechnology (EV-Biotech)
column6:
This proposal builds on the prior government investment in the Eastern Visayas Innovation Center for Health Biotechnology (EV-Biotech) building, approved in 2025 and expected to be completed in 2026.  It will turn this new facility into a fully operational regional innovation hub for disease prevention and health security.  The project will establish and equip advanced biotechnology laboratory systems at Visayas State University to support the full research, instruction, extension, and innovation (RIEI) continuum. In line with the original EV-Biotech concept, it will address priority infectious and emerging diseases and add climate- and disaster-associated diseases in Eastern Visayas as a key focus area.  This responds to the growing impact of strong typhoons, earthquakes, and other natural hazards in the region and to lessons from the recent global pandemic. It is designed to provide concrete, science-based solutions to emerging health risks and trends.
The project will install and integrate molecular diagnostics and genomics platforms (nucleic acid extraction, conventional and real-time PCR, sequencing-ready workflows), immunoassay and serology facilities (ELISA, cell culture), environmental and vector-borne disease laboratories, and biobanking infrastructure for long-term sample storage. It will also deploy digital laboratory information management and analytics systems that can interface with regional disease surveillance mechanisms.  These systems will be used to develop, validate, and deploy locally appropriate diagnostic assays and biosurveillance tools for flood- and landslide-associated diseases such as leptospirosis, dengue and other vector-borne infections, water- and food-borne diseases and support work on other priority infectious and emerging threats identified in the original proposal.  This will complement existing DOH and regional laboratories by focusing on innovation, method development, and specialized testing that address current gaps in regional health security.
Building on these capacities, EV-Biotech will implement multi-disciplinary, One Health–oriented research programs that link human, animal, and environmental health. Priority areas include climate- and disaster-associated infectious diseases, antimicrobial resistance in clinical, environmental, and agricultural settings, low-cost rapid tests and point-of-care diagnostics for LGUs and rural health units, and biomarkers of vulnerability, nutrition, and immunity in at-risk populations.  Geospatial and data science approaches will be used to integrate laboratory, environmental, and epidemiologic data.  The resulting decision-support tools will help LGUs and health planners improve risk assessment, early warning, and targeting of interventions before, during, and after disaster events.
The Center will be embedded in VSU’s academic and training programs and will also serve the wider Eastern Visayas Health Research and Development Consortium (EVHRDC).  Advanced diagnostics, biosafety, climate–health linkages, and One Health concepts will be integrated into relevant curricula at VSU and capacity-building activities for EVHRDC member institutions.  EV-Biotech will host undergraduate and graduate theses, practicums, and internships, and will offer specialized training for faculty, researchers, medical technologists, and LGU health workers from VSU and other EVHRDC partners.  These activities will strengthen regional competencies in molecular diagnostics, biosurveillance, and data-driven health decision-making.
To ensure sustainability and long-term impact, the proposal will establish pipelines for technology development and transfer.  These will include locally developed diagnostic kits, reagents, biosensors, and decision-support tools.  The project will formalize partnership frameworks with national and local government agencies, SUCs, and the private sector.  Internal systems for management, monitoring and evaluation, and quality assurance will be institutionalized to maintain operational efficiency and compliance with national and international standards.  Through these interventions, EV-Biotech will progress from a newly completed physical facility into a sustainable regional platform for disease prevention and health security, with a clear focus on climate- and disaster-related risks.  It will contribute directly to national and regional development priorities and to SDGs 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), 9 (Industry, Innovation and Infrastructure), and 13 (Climate Action).

column4: Digital Transformation Centers (DTC)
column5: Department of Information and Communications Technology
column6:
The DTC Project represents a progressive iteration of the TechED Cr Project, a national
initiative aimed at digital inclusion. The primary objective of this project is to establish a
network of nationwide self-sustaining centers, delivering ongoing Government and
ICT-enabled services to empower underserved or unserved communities.
DTCs can be implemented in various settings, including barangays, municipalities, or
remote areas, to offer crucial ICT-enabled services such as internet access, eGovernment
services, and digital skills training. Operated by a diverse array of partners, including
Local Government Units (LGUs), public libraries, State-Universities and Colleges
(SUCs), Non-Government Organizations (NGOS), and private institutions, DTCs are
dedicated to advancing digital literacy and fostering inclusion from the grassroots level,
targeting urban, semi-urban populations, Geographically Disadvantaged and Isolated
Areas (GIDA), and Last-Mile and areas where fundamental, low-advanced digital
training is required.

DTCs serve as training hubs, delivering a wide range of digital skills development
programs, from basic to advanced levels. Concentrating on upskilling the youth,
Indigenous People (IP), Persons With Disability (PWD), Out-of-School Youth (OSY),
Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMI's) and entrepreneurs, elderly,
government employees, digital job seekers, and other members of the community,
ensuring that the training offered corresponds with the local industry requirements and
economic prospects.
The DTC Project comprises three key components: Physical, Virtual, and Human, each
integral to achieving its goal of fostering digital inclusion and empowerment for
unserved and underserved communities across the nation
Physical
It comprises venues for training and collaboration.
Types of Digital Transformation Centers
Digital Transformation Centers are classified into two types:
● DICT-Owned DCs are facilities owned and operated by the department.
● Partner-Owned DCs are facilities owned and operated by partner institutions
and organizations. Partner-owned centers can be further classified, but are not
limited to the following center models:
○ Local Government Unit (LGU)
○ Public Library
○ School
○ Alternative Learning System (ALS)
○ State Universities and Colleges (SUC)
○ Farmers IT Services (FITS) Center
○ Negosyo Center
○ Correctional Facility
○ Rural Impact Sourcing (RIS) Hub
○ Civil Society
○ Mobile Tech4ED Center, and others.
DTCs have four (4) levels.

Level 1 DTC
A Level 1 DTC has one (1) training room of approximately 36 square meters.
This compact yet functional area is equipped with at least ten (10) workstations, with
one (1) designated workstation for Persons with Disabilities (PWD). The layout optimizes the limited space to accommodate essential equipment and foster a conducive
learning environment.
The training room can serve as a space for instructors to prepare lessons, grade
assignments, consult with students, and collaborate with colleagues, and the acquisition
of basic digital literacy by the elderly, PWDs, Indigenous Groups, and out-of-school
youth (OSYs) and low-income individuals.
Level 2 DTC
Level 2 DTC is proposed to have at least a 250 square meter lot area that is equipped
with one (1) training room, which has at least 25 workstations, and two
(2) designated workstations for PWDs. Additionally, the center features one (1)
multi-purpose room that can be used as a conference room or co-working space, and
various ancillary spaces to support its operations.
The center can serve as a facility for conducting workshops and offering intermediate
digital skills training, such as digital marketing and digital communications tools, and
may include web development, software programming languages, data analysis, and
project management software, among others.
Level 3 DTC
Level 3 DCs are proposed to have at least a 540 square meter lot area with three
(3) ICT training rooms equipped with at least 25 workstations each, one (1)
multi-purpose room that can be used as a conference room or co-working space, one (1)
Administration Office serves as the hub for organizational tasks, and an open space that
promotes collaboration.
The center serves as a facility for conducting workshops and may offer advanced digital
skills training, such as Network Design, Cybersecurity.
Software Development, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and Machine Learning (ML).
Users may also access support programs, mentorship, and resources for local MSMEs
and startups.

Level 4 DTC
Level 4 DTCs integrates specialized spaces: an ICTA training room for tech-driven
education, a flexible Co-Working space for diverse professionals, a Point of Presence
ensuring network connectivity, a Shared Support office for centralized administration,
private offices for focused tasks, a Repair/Technical Support room for maintenance, and
Specialized Department offices tailored for areas like environmental protection and
health services. The center is proposed to have at least a 1,000 square meter lot area that
is equipped with three (3) ICI training room is a tech-equipped space for ICT learning,
one (1) shared support services, one (1) multi-purpose room that can be used as
conference room or co-working space, one (1) Administration Office serves, (1) cafeteria, one (1) specialized department", one (1) repair and technical support and one (1) DTC
office.
Level 4 DTCs may be determined after:
● The conduct of Needs-based Analysis of the industries and communities of the
DTC (consider industries of Digital Cities and results from Digital Skills
Mapping of RA 11927).
● The identification of specialization/s in partnership with the academe and
industries that will equip DCs with the necessary capability and equipment to
deliver these services, as well as conduct Research and Development activities.
Virtual
To complement the physical spaces and facilities and to support the operational and
reportorial needs of the DCs, virtual services, tools, and platforms are implemented and
integrated. The Tech4ED-DTC Platform is the digital gateway of all capacity
development initiatives of the ICT Literacy and Competency Development Bureau
(ILCDB) and has the necessary features for the efficient and effective delivery of
capacity development programs and center operations.
Tech4ED - DTC Platform
The platform includes the following components:
Client-Facing
Learning and Skills Development Module - This provides all users with a centralized
enrollment and training system where users can schedule upskilling and reskilling
courses from the Learning Management System (LMS) and the Learning Experience
Portal (LXP). It allows learners to view a calendar of courses and a profile of all ongoing
and accomplished courses. This also enables access to external partner systems and
content, including learning management systems, content databases, and other training
materials and resources. Notable partner platforms include the CISCO Networking
Academy, HP LIFE, through an ITU partnership. 

Service Integration Module - This provides third-party partners to link or integrate their
systems to the platform to further enhance the experience of people availing
The services in the Tech4ED-DTCs. Offerings include the National Government Portal
(NGP) or e-Gov Portal and Single-Sign On capabilities, and other future government
systems made available to the public.
Administration and Analytics
Center Operations Modules - This provides administrative and managerial access to
Center Managers for user account management, monitoring of center operations, and
equipment access and inventory. A centralized module that allows real-time access and
reporting across the board.

Data Analytics and Reports Modules - This provides the capability to extract insight
from learning behavior, center and staff data, center utilization, and other data points
that will support center managers, trainers, the Tech4ED-DTC Project Management
Team (PMT), and relevant stakeholders, including Senior Executive Officials for ICT
capacity-building efforts. This enables data-driven decision-making for operations,
reports, and insight generation for stakeholders.
Human
Activities
The stakeholders, center managers, and clients in the community need

column4: Modification of Hybrid Electric Road Train (HERT) Energy Storage System (ESS) Using Lithium-Ion Batteries (Phase 2 - Kidapawan)
column5: Metals Industry Research and Development Center
column6:
The Hybrid Electric Road Train (HERT) research and development project, led by the Department of Science and Technology - Metals Industry Research and Development Center (DOST-MIRDC), aims to address traffic and environmental challenges in the Philippines. The HERT introduces a hybrid electric vehicle powered by a combination of a diesel generator and lead-acid batteries, improving fuel efficiency and reducing the environmental impact compared to traditional vehicles. However, the current lead-acid battery system faces challenges such as maintenance issues due to the large number of batteries, a limited lifespan, and the need for frequent replacements. Despite these drawbacks, lead-acid batteries were initially chosen for their cost-effectiveness.

A promising alternative to the lead-acid batteries is the use of lithium-ion batteries. These offer superior safety, longevity, and a significantly lower environmental impact. Lithium-ion batteries require fewer units to provide the same capacity as lead-acid batteries, leading to reduced maintenance and operational costs. They also have a longer lifespan, reducing the need for frequent replacements. Moreover, lithium-ion batteries are environmentally friendly, safer, and can be placed more flexibly within the vehicle.

This upgrade aligns with the environmental goals of the project, and the batteries also support the UP CHRG Electric Vehicle Technologies, Inc. project, “Rapid Electric Vehicle Charging - Charging in Minutes (CharM),” enhancing the HERT’s charging system. Additionally, transferring the HERT to Kidapawan City, North Cotabato, will improve the local transportation system by offering a safer, more efficient, and aesthetically appealing public transit option.

column4: Advancing Food Security, Health, and Nutrition with Alternative Staple Food Innovations
column5: University of Science and Technology of Southern Philippines
column6: Food security is a fundamental human right and a cornerstone of sustainable development. In the recent Global Food Security Index, the global food environment has continued to exhibit deterioration which has threatened food security.  In particular, the Philippines dropped from rank 64 down to 67 out of 113 countries in the 2022 Global Food Security Index measured in terms of its four dimensions: availability, quality, safety, affordability, and sustainability and adaptation. The imminent risks from the prevailing pandemic effects, increasing population pressures, climate change, and resource depletion will continue to impact food security in the future. hence, efforts on the adoption of innovative solutions are essential to address these issues. As part of the stakeholders, the University of Science and Technology of Southern Philippines - Claveria (USTP-Claveria) can play a pivotal role in advancing food security and sustainability through research, development, and science and technology (S&T) initiatives. In support of this, initiatives to strengthen and address challenges in food security and sustainability are incorporated in this proposal. This proposal emphasizes the significant role of agricultural and food innovations as drivers in ensuring food security. It seeks to enhance agricultural productivity, improve food quality, reduce environmental impact, and strengthen local food systems by providing improved research and development and fostering innovative solutions. This can be done through capacity-building activities for researchers, and enhancement of the current technologies and facilities available in the university. Moreover, launching pilot programs in agricultural communities and technology transfer can be done to boost agricultural productivity and promote economic growth.  To further support farmers and local communities, the proposal includes training programs and workshops focused on sustainable agricultural practices, food safety, and resource management. Through a collaborative approach that combines research, technology, and community engagement, this initiative seeks to transform agricultural practices, ensuring food systems are not only more productive but also resilient and sustainable. Overall, the objectives of this proposal are in line with the Department of Science and Technology's Harmonized National R&D Agenda for 2022-2028, as well as the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 2 on Zero Hunger and SDG 12 on Responsible Consumption and Production. Additionally, the emphasis on food security is consistent with the priorities outlined in the Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 and the Philippine Food Systems Transformation Pathway, highlighting the significance of this focus.

1.        Solids Energy Materials Laboratory. This unit will provide capability for detailed characterization of biomass and solid fuels, including proximate and ultimate analysis, calorimetry, ash behavior profiling, thermal decomposition assessment (TGA), and feedstock preparation. These analyses are critical for biomass gasifier design, combustion modeling, waste-to-energy optimization, and industry certifications. Current regional limitations in solids testing hinder accurate evaluation of agricultural residues, wood fuels, and waste-derived biomass.

2.        Liquid Energy Materials Laboratory. This laboratory will enhance USTP’s capacity to evaluate biofuels and liquid intermediates such as biodiesel, pyrolysis oil, alcohol blends, and other renewable energy liquids. The facility addresses gaps in viscosity, density, calorific value, flash point, oxidation stability, and chemical composition testing—parameters required to meet DOE, ASTM, and international standards. Improved liquid fuel testing ensures quality control, safety, and efficiency for transport, industrial heating, and local biofuel production systems.

3.        Gaseous-State Energy Analysis Laboratory. This unit focuses on advanced analysis of biogas, syngas, and other gaseous fuels. It will enable methane–carbon dioxide–hydrogen sulfide quantification, real-time emissions profiling, engine/generator performance evaluation, and gas conditioning system validation. Accurate gas analysis is essential for waste-to-energy deployment, industrial emissions compliance, and the development of clean, climate-friendly fuel technologies. This component directly supports the validation of PSA purification units, thermal conversion systems, and emerging green energy applications.

Combined, these three laboratories form a unified energy materials testing platform that addresses a long-standing regional infrastructure gap in Mindanao. Current laboratory facilities are insufficient to support advanced testing for biomass gasification, fuel certification, clean-energy systems modeling, and emissions diagnostics. Upgrading the Energy Testing and Analysis Laboratory fills this gap by providing accessible, high-quality analytical services for LGUs, industries, cooperatives, and academic researchers.

Alignment with the Philippine Development Plan (PDP)
The project strongly supports PDP 2023–2028 priorities, including:
•        Clean and sustainable energy transition, through improved validation of renewable fuels and low-emission systems.
•        Green industry development, by enabling local industries to meet energy efficiency and environmental compliance requirements.
•        Circular bioeconomy advancement, via enhanced biomass characterization and waste-to-energy evaluation.
•        Innovation-driven and climate-resilient regional growth, through strengthened R&D capability and reduced dependence on facilities outside Mindanao.

Overall Purpose of the Facility Upgrade
The upgraded laboratory will serve as the analytical backbone for renewable energy innovation, technology validation, emissions compliance, and regional capacity-building. It forms a strategic foundation for long-term research, teaching, extension, and industry support—positioning USTP as Northern Mindanao’s leading institution for energy systems testing and analysis.

column4: WAstewater Treatment by Environment-friendly solutions from Radiation technology (WATER)
column5: Philippine Council for Industry, Energy and Emerging Technology Research and Development
column6:
In 2017, NEDA reported that over 10% of the Philippine population lacked access to clean water and sanitation, hindering progress toward UN-SDG 6. To address this, the PCIEERD S&T Water Environment Roadmap was created to support water conservation and management. A critical gap identified is the lack of advanced treatment technologies to meet national effluent standards (DAO 2016-08 and 2021-19), particularly for nutrient contaminants like nitrates, phosphates, and sulfates. Additionally, alarming levels of heavy metals—such as manganese, cadmium, lead, and arsenic—have been detected in water sources across the country.

Current treatment methods, relying on biological agents, flocculants, and resins, face limitations in efficiency, increased waste generation, and operational complexity. This project proposes the development of advanced, sustainable adsorbents using radiation-induced graft polymerization (RIGP), a green technology that produces functional materials tailored for specific contaminants. The goal is to create column prototype units that are easy to integrate, cost-effective, and highly reusable, enabling industries to comply with water quality standards while minimizing environmental impact.

column4: Post-radiation Reactive Extrusion of Plastic Waste (PREx Plastic)
column5: Philippine Council for Industry, Energy and Emerging Technology Research and Development
column6:
One major challenge in plastic recycling is the limited use of post-consumer recycled (PCR) plastics in manufacturing due to their lower quality. These materials often have inferior properties, making them suitable only for blending with small amounts of virgin plastics or for low-value products, which is financially unsustainable due to high processing costs. As a result, local manufacturers prefer to import virgin plastics. For mechanical recycling to be profitable, the recycled products must have high performance and market potential.

Radiation processing technology offers a solution by improving the properties of polymers through methods like crosslinking, scission, and graft copolymerization. A technique called Post-radiation Reactive Extrusion (PREx) uses irradiation to modify PCR plastics like PP and PE, enhancing their thermo-mechanical properties through interfacial grafting and compatibilization. This process can produce high-performance materials suitable for applications like housing construction.

By establishing ICITES, USTP aims to revolutionize how innovation and entrepreneurship are integrated into education. column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: The vegetable production systems in the country are intensively managed and are prone to a series of biophysical constraints that greatly impact productivity and sustainability. The previous ACIAR project on vegetable production (SMCN/2012/029) has identified major gaps in our understanding of the short- and long-term impacts of crop management practices on soil fertility and off-site environmental impacts. Specifically, these included undiagnosed micronutrient deficiencies, excessive soil accumulation of Cu and Zn, and excessive application of fertilizer and manures. Rates of fertilizer application were greatly in excess of crop demand and the seasonal application of Cu and Zn through fungicides was found to be in the order of 20-30 times crop demand. column4: Development of Microbial and Plant-Microbial Combinations for Bioremediation of Pesticide Contaminated Vegetables Areas in Selected Provinces
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Benguet farming areas and vegetables have been reported to be contaminated with varied pesticide residues, with chlorpyrifos being one of the highest and commonly detected in vegetables and soil (Reyes & Laurean, 2007; Lu, 2010; Ngidlo, 2013).  Preliminary studies done to isolate microbes, particularly endophytic bacteria from persistently contaminated farms in La Trinidad, Benguet had yielded a number of species with extremely high tolerance to chlorpyrifos and some with moderate capacity for degradation in vitro. These were identified by 16s rDNA sequencing as Acinetobacter junii, Kosakonia sacchari, K. oryzendophytica, Pseudomonas monteilii, Raoultella ornithinolytica, Pseudomonas stutzeri, Enterobacter kobei, E. asburiae, E. cloacae, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Pantoea agglomerans (Guyo and Tipayno, 2021). This research intends to use indigenous populations of pesticide degrading microorganisms and associated plants in developing formulations for the purpose of reducing pesticide residues in selected contaminated vegetables areas in Benguet, creating a safer environment at the same time improving soil health and productivity. The first phase consists of isolating fungal, soil and endophytic bacterial populations with high tolerance and degradation capacity for organophosphate pesticides commonly detected in Benguet vegetables

column4: Development and Evaluation of Soil Fertility and Nutrient Management Strategies for Hybrid Coconut Farming in Eastern Visayas
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6:
In coconut production it is imperative to monitor the essential nutrients present in the soil.
This project involves three components: (1) evaluation of the soil properties and fertility status
grown with coconut in Region VIII; (2) determination of Critical Nutrient Levels of hybrid
coconuts and (3) evaluation and efficacy testing of different fertilizer combinations (INM
approach) based on soil-test results for hybrid coconut production. This project will provide
available soil fertility data, coconut suitability maps, identify the critical nutrient levels of N, P and

column4: Ploidy-dependent physiological and chemical traits of Kappaphycus cultivars Project 1.  Prevalence and ploidy-dependent physiological responses in farmed cultivars and novel strains of Kappaphycus
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Ploidy is the number of complete sets of chromosomes in a cell or an organism, which can either be monoploid (=haploid; 1 set), diploid (2 sets), or polyploid (3 or more chromosome sets). Variation in ploidy confers adaptive and ecological significance. For example, among unicellular organisms, haploids are less fit than diploids following exposure to mutagens but are more fit than diploids under certain nutrient limited conditions, but not under others. Polyploids are common among plants and green algae but are less adequately documented in red and brown algae. Increasing ploidy level is suggested to improve plant traits such as size, quality, yield, enhanced vigor, and improved tolerances to environmental stresses, pests, and pathogens. Whether this is true among our farmed eucheumatoids remained to be investigated. This study will determine the prevalence of ploidy corresponding to specific life history phase among commercial and novel Kappaphycus strains, and their corresponding physiological and biochemical characteristics. Unravelling the occurrence and prevalence of specific ploidy in Kappaphycus is important in: (1) understanding corresponding vigor and productivity among different cultivars; (2) selecting novel strains from the wild for future domestication replacing old and fatigued cultivars; and (3) developing tools for breeding and crop improvement programs.

The Textile Academy provides the necessary platform for PTRI to champion human capital development in a highly technical and specialized field like textiles. column4: Establishment of Embedded and Mechatronics Simulation Laboratory
column6:
The establishment of our Embedded Systems & Mechatronics Simulation Laboratory marks a significant leap forward in engineering education and research. This cutting-edge facility is meticulously designed to serve as a hub for exploration, experimentation, and collaboration at the intersection of embedded systems and mechatronics.
Equipped with state-of-the-art hardware components such as advanced microcontrollers, sensors, actuators, and communication modules, alongside a suite of industry-standard simulation software including MATLAB/Simulink, LabVIEW, and SolidWorks, the laboratory offers a comprehensive platform for students, researchers, and industry professionals to delve into the complexities of intelligent systems.
Through hands-on experimentation, students will not only gain practical skills in designing, programming, and testing embedded systems but also develop a deep understanding of mechatronics principles and their applications in real-world scenarios. Leveraging this intellectual capital, the Council recognizes the strategic importance of transferring knowledge, skills, and innovative practices to its emerging members—an essential step in strengthening its collegial function and sustaining national research excellence.

By integrating scientific training with organizational development, CASCaDe-ME ensures that enhanced competencies translate into meaningful contributions to research, policy formulation, and regional development.

These efforts are aligned with NRCP’s core mandate: to promote and support basic research, enhance research capability, foster interdisciplinary linkages, cultivate a scientific and technological culture, and serve as a policy advisory body to the government.

To maintain a robust pipeline of talent in Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI), it is imperative to create a nurturing environment that empowers young Filipinos to become future leaders in science and technology. This program specifically targets promising early-career researchers, providing them with opportunities to conduct basic research on self-initiated topics within the funding scope of DOST-NRCP.

Properly rehabilitating and sustainably managing these mangrove resources can yield a multitude of environmental, social, and economic advantages, essential for the resilience of coastal communities and the broader ecosystem.

Revitalized mangroves serve as a formidable barrier, safeguarding lives, properties, and critical infrastructure like fishing ports and agricultural lands. They shield coastal areas from the escalating threats of storm surges, erosion, and saltwater intrusion driven by rising sea levels and extreme weather events. Mangroves act as potent carbon sinks, absorbing significant amounts of carbon dioxide. Expanding mangrove cover aligns with climate change mitigation efforts, helping combat global warming and reducing the region's carbon footprint, vital for international climate commitments and sustainable development goals. Also, mangroves harbor rich biodiversity, providing a haven for various endangered and endemic flora and fauna. Rehabilitation efforts contribute to biodiversity conservation, bolstering ecological equilibrium and supporting broader marine and terrestrial ecosystems.

column4: Harnessing Abaca Genetic Resources: Integrating Molecular Strategies for Pest Management, Drought Resiliency, and On-site Detection Assays  Project 1. Profiling, genetic, and functional analysis of abaca (Musa textilis Nee) responses to drought and bunchy top disease stresses
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6:
Due to the decline in abaca fiber production owing to biotic and abiotic stresses (Ocfemia Buhay, 1934; Arcalas, 2020), there is a need to characterize and identify varieties that are resilient to abiotic (drought) and biotic (ABTV and BBTV) stresses. This project seeks to study the biology and genetic diversity of M. frugalis, as well as that of other lepidopteran species that are potentially emerging or transboundary pests of sugarcane. Finally, the species of hymenopteran parasitoids present in the area will be identified and their potential as biological control agents will be assessed. column4: Harnessing Adaptive Responses and Best Practices against Fall Armyworm using Science and Technology (HARABUST) Community-based mass production and utilization of biological control agents against armyworm of sugarcane, corn and  onion
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Sugarcane farming in the Philippines faces significant challenges due to low productivity and the increasing prevalence of pests and diseases. One of the most pressing threats is the invasive fall armyworm (FAW), Spodoptera frugiperda, which has caused widespread damage to sugarcane and corn fields across the country. In Negros Occidental, FAW infestation has devastated up to 923.5 hectares of crops, with 100% damage reported in Himamaylan. Affected plants exhibited severe symptoms, including skeletonized leaves and damaged shoots, posing a serious threat to sugarcane production. To combat this issue, biological control offers a sustainable solution. Natural predators such as predatory earwigs, and hymenopterous parasitoids like Telenomus remus and Trichogramma species, play a crucial role in regulating FAW populations. These biological control agents (BCAs) have demonstrated high parasitism rates, with co-existent parasitism reaching 84.4%. Mass production protocols for earwigs and Trichogramma are already established, while T. remus production is being optimized. A community-based mass production and utilization of these BCAs is proposed as a sustainable approach to managing FAW infestations in sugarcane. Utilizing biological control can mitigate the damage caused by FAW and improve sugarcane productivity in affected regions.

column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: The recently reported infestation of the fall armyworm (FAW), Spodoptera frugiperda, in Negros province seriously affected the Philippine sugarcane and corn industries. Sugarcane production supports the livelihood of 13,039 planters in the region. Meanwhile, 1,683 hectares planted to corn in Negros Oriental were currently reported infested by FAW. An environment-friendly pest management option is crucial for the sustainable management of this pest on sugarcane and corn. Nucleopolyhedroviruses (NPV) have been proven effective and safe biological control agents against lepidopterous pests. To date, several native NPV isolates that infect different Spodoptera species has been reported but none has been naturally isolated from FAW in the country These native NPV cause moderate to high mortality to FAW under laboratory conditions. The variation in their virulence could be attributed to the genotypic strains in the wild-type isolates. In addition, their restrictive host range and inconsistent field efficacy are considered limiting factors for their widespread utilization as biopesticides. A recent technology with custom-designed mixtures of NPV strains improved their virulence in certain insects. Thus, this project aims to improve the virulence of native Spodopteran NPV strains against FAW through interspecific and intraspecific coocclusion technology and serial passages (Gain-of-Function Research) in local FAW populations.

In addition to pheromone traps, light traps are considered a potential option for mass trapping of FAW, although only a few studies have evaluated their effectiveness. This proposed project aims to evaluate the performance of different trapping systems for the monitoring and control of FAW. It also seeks to integrate these technologies into integrated pest management (IPM) strategies to promote sustainable farming practices and reduce reliance on synthetic pesticides.

column4: Harnessing Adaptive Responses and Best Practices against Fall Armyworm using Science and Technology (HARABUST) Optimization of Solid-state Cultivation of Armyworm Control Agent, Metarhizium rileyi
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Armyworms are invasive insect pests in the Philippines causing severe damage to crops, lowering quality and income for farmers. The fall armyworm (FAW, Spodoptera frugiperda) was first reported causing severe damage to corn plants in the Philippines in 2019. Since then, it has expanded its range and now infests major crops such as rice and sugarcane. Recently, FAW destroyed 558.23 hectares of sugarcane and corn fields in several municipalities in Negros. The widespread occurrence of FAW warrants immediate deployment of control measures and biological control agents to suppress the damaging pest population. One of the known and promising fungal pathogen of FAW is Metarhizium rileyi. Extensive studies have been done at NCPC to ascertain its virulence against FAW and other armyworm species, and its characterization and initial mass production. This proposed initiative aims to develop cost-effective, adaptable, and scalable cultivation methods through optimizing physico-chemical and biological parameters. Production of M. rileyi via solid-state fermentation offers a sustainable and community-driven approach to pest management. This initiative aligns with the DOST Pillars and promotes human wellbeing in food and agriculture, potentially reducing the use of synthetic insecticides and promoting sustainable pest mitigation.

The genome information will be used to identify the uniqueness of the Philippine TRVs, find similarities and variations, and look for novel traits and genes. Moreover, the genomic data will be used by the other project in the program, to associate the genetic variants with specific traits. The traits of interest are herbicide tolerance, earliness, low phytic acid, micronutrient-dense rice, high-quality protein rice, and anaerobic seed germination. The project will lead to the identification of rice accessions which can be used as donor parents or be sources of novel alleles for rice improvement programs. Eventually, this may result in the development of rice cultivars that are more nutritious and resilient to the effects of climate change.

column6:
Climate change possesses significant challenges to sugarcane production in the Philippines. The technology transfer process involves various steps including idea generation and technology development; assessment and patenting of the technology; market study and valuation; and building of university-industry collaboration through informal and formal linkage means and processes. One particular strategy in the technology transfer process is patent mining which aims to develop and promote positive changes in research and development (R&D) programs and prioritize emerging technologies and key commodities in the agriculture, aquatic, and natural resources (AANR) sector. Patent mining banks on various patent literature, through early IP management strategies, and serves as a guide for organizations in planning for targeted R&D investments.

The technology transfer process concludes with the transfer of the university-generated intellectual properties (IPs) to the industry partner committed to utilizing and commercializing these technologies. In some cases, this industry partner is a start-up business, or a small company working to solve a problem where the solution is not obvious. They are smaller, more agile businesses that have the potential to grow at an exponential rate, but they are temporary since their end goal is always to exit – or to become a full-fledged company.

column4: Bamboo Resources Inventory and Technology-Enabled Mapping in the Philippines (BRITEMAP). Project 3. Imperatives of Policy and Leveraging Stakeholders and National Entities towards Institutionalizing BRITEMAP (IMPLEMENT BRITEMAP)
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6:
The growth of the bamboo industry is hindered due to lack of reliable and updated bamboo information. Despite initiatives of the different agencies like DENR and DTI-PBIDC, bamboo information remained inaccessible, lacking and outdated.

The BRITEMAP Program is proposing a technology system of an inventory system and information sharing scheme that will provide accurate, reliable and accessible bamboo resource information. In order for the technology to become sustainable and functional, it is proposed that an institution should be created that is mandated to adopt and implement the proposed bamboo inventory and information system.

The formulation of the policy will involve the creation of a Technical Working Group consisting of representatives from the DENR, DA, DTI-PBIDC & DILG. Series of public consultations shall be conducted as a participatory approach in the formulation of the proposed policy.

column4: Improved Pollination Intensity for Increased Cacao Yields
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Cacao is an important high-value crop in the Philippines. It is the raw material of chocolates and other intermediate products with no available substitute. But with inadequate production, the global industry is faced with a supply deficit that continues to increase every year. The Philippine Cacao Industry thus created The Philippine Cacao Industry Roadmap (2021-2025) that updated the 2017-2022 Roadmap. The new roadmap contains innovations to realign its vision, mission, goals, strategies and interventions with relevant national and international policies and frameworks including the Agriculture and Fisheries Modernization Act of 1997, the United Nation's Sustainable Development Goals, the AmBisyon Natin 2040, the Philippine Development Plan, and the proposed Philippine Cacao Industry Development Act. Several strategies and interventions were suggested to enhance farm productivity and promote the transition to organic farming practices.

column4: Socio-Ecological Assessment of the Invertebrate Gleaning Fisheries in the Philippines Towards Evidence-based Sustainable Resource Governance (GleanPhil Program). Project 1: Gleaning Fisheries as a Valuable Food System: Socio-demographics, Fisheries Production, Food Security, and Nutrition of Coastal Communities
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Gleaning fisheries, characterized by the collection of seafood resources from intertidal areas, play a crucial role in the food security of coastal communities dependent on subsistence fishing. Gleaning, however, is given less priority in the Philippine government's research, development, and management programs. Appropriate attention to this sector and the provision of science-based evidence to support a policy framework are urgently needed to prevent overharvesting of nearshore seafood resources. There is also a need to highlight the adoption of a community-based participatory research approach as well as gender roles and their contribution to small-scale fisheries production. The main goal of the project is to obtain reliable, comprehensive, and sex-aggregated information on the social and economic values of gleaning fisheries to support formulation of management measures toward sustainable utilization of macroinvertebrate resources in the Philippines. The project’s main focus is on the socio-demographic profile of gleaners, the production and economic values of invertebrate fisheries, and their contribution to food security and nutrient adequacy of the gleaning households. The project results will provide valuable input to formulating policy recommendations toward the sustainability of the gleaning fisheries and their myriad benefits to marginalized coastal communities in the country.

column4: Isolation, Characterization, and Utilization of Functional Microbes in Fermentation and Physico-Chemical Analysis of Fermented Cacao Beans for Improved Quality
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6:
Current practices of cacao beans fermentation in the Philippines generally generated inferior quality fermented beans based on the results of studies under NICER Cacao R&D Center. There is a need to develop fermentation protocols to generate high quality fermented beans. Functional microbes play significant roles in fermentation leading to enhanced and improved bean quality. There is a need to isolate, identify, and functionally characterize the microbes for utility in fermentation of cacao beans. There is also a need to develop other strategies for enhanced fermentation and increased quality of beans. To ensure production of quality fermented cacao beans, there is a need to assess the grade, sensory and physico-chemical properties of the processed beans.

The project is expected produce high-quality fermented cacao beans that command higher prices and increased profits for cacao farmer and processors; increase in demand of Philippine cacao fermented bean in domestic and export markets; and production of superior quality chocolates, tablea and other cacao-based value-added products both locally and internationally.

column4: Socio-Ecological Assessment of the Invertebrate Gleaning Fisheries in the Philippines Towards Evidence-based Sustainable Resource Governance (GleanPhil Program). Project 2: Gleaning Habitat and Biodiversity Assessment and Biology of Commercially Exploited Marine Invertebrates
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Despite the importance of gleaning fisheries as a source of food and supplemental income, the ecological and biological dynamics of seafood resources remain inadequately studied. The proposed project focuses on studying the ecology, biology and aspects of the population dynamics of commercially important species collected by gleaning in selected sites of the Philippines. A description of the gleaning habitats, diversity of macroinvertebrates therein, and relevant ecological information of the various sites will be provided in the project through employing fisheries-independent survey techniques. General information on the biology of the identified target species from each site will be explored, including information on species' gonad condition and some aspects of their population dynamics. Investigations on ecology and biology are crucial to help us better appreciate these resources and understand their dynamics to ultimately help in crafting rational management guidelines for their sustainable utilization. Utilization of these species for food and income shall be covered by the gleaning fisheries component of this research program. Altogether, this information provides input to the crafting of management guidelines for the sound utilization of these commercially important gleaned resources in the country.

column4: Propagation and conservation of the top priority plants in the forests over limestone of Samar Island Natural Park, Samar Island, Philippines
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6:
This project proposal will provide insight into the propagation of the top priority species for conservation in the forests over limestone of Samar Island Natural Park (SINP). The top priority species were identified by Buot et al. (2024) based on their harvesting risk, economic and cultural uses, and species distribution and frequency values. Most of these priority plants are understudied, hence information related to their propagation are lacking. Inability to reproduce these species may lead to their decline and possible extinction. Thus, it is important to determine the best propagation method that will allow us to conserve and use these priority species in a sustainable manner.  

Propagation of the top priority plants for conservation will be an effective technique for increasing and sustaining the population size of these species in SINP. This study will also provide a better understanding of the biology of the top priority species. Furthermore, the findings of this study will be communicated to stakeholders to ensure the reintroduction of the priority species in their area and to promote plant propagation as a potential source of income for the local communities.

column4: Prospecting Natural Insecticides and Preservatives: Phytochemical Analysis, Insecticidal Activity and Preservative Potential of Extracts from Tropical Trees and Weedy Plant Species Against Powder Post Beetles (Dinoderus minutus Fabricius)
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: The project is in support to the NICER Bamboo Research and Development Center of Central Mindanao University (BRDC-CMU), which is a collaborative endeavor aligned with the Bamboo S&T Roadmap particularly on the development of novel products. This research will focus on exploring four tropical trees and five invasive weedy plant species that have potentials as natural insecticides against bamboo borers specifically powder post beetle or PPB (Dinoderus minutus Fabricius). As a multipurpose and economically important crop for the country, it is essential therefore to address the threats (e.g. biotic threats) that might affect the quality and service life-span of bamboo and its derived products.

This will contribute to the general picture of gleaning in the country. Data will be collected using mixed-methods and will be analyzed using descriptive statistics.

column4: Saving the Globally Important and Critically Endangered Lycophyte, Isoetes philippinensis Merr. & Perry (Isoetaceae) in Olangu River, Lanao del Norte
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: The critically endangered and site endemic lycophyte, Isoetes philippinensis has global importance because it is the only species in the Philippines and found nowhere else in the world. It was reported to be extinct in the wild as it was not observed and recollected after 1969 until rediscovered in May 25, 2022 (Amoroso et al. 2022). Since the biology of this species has not been investigated for its potential medicinal and other economic uses, the physico-chemical properties will likewise be studied.

column4: Survey, Propagation, and Conservation of Philippine Native Taxus Species (Taxus wallichiana Zucc.)
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6:
Taxus is known worldwide as source of Taxol, an anti-cancer drug. The species native to the Philippines is Taxus wallichiana Zucc., which was reportedly been exploited for the taxol extraction.  Other potential uses of Taxus are its essential oil with increasing demand abroad. The high costs of essential oil resulted to rampant illegal collection, decreasing population, and inclusion of Taxus in DAO 2017-11 (National List of Threatened Philippine Plants) and CITES (Conservation on International Trade Endangered Species). As of to date, there is no existing data on the distribution nor policies specific for Taxus harvesting and collection. Publications on the potential uses, chemical characterization, propagation, and threats are limited despite of its promising uses for medicinal uses and economic value.

To address this gaps, resource survey and mapping will be conducted to determine the geographical distribution of T. wallichiana. Meanwhile, different methods and treatments will be tested to develop the Taxus propagation protocol. Several interviews, capacity buildings and trainings will be conducted to capacitate the local communities in the protection and conservation of Taxus in their areas.

column4: Access and Benefit Sharing Policy Options for the Sustainable Management of Batanes Protected Landscapes and Seascapes (ABS Batanes)
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: The declaration of Batanes as a protected area brought about many benefits that contributed to the conservation of the province’s unique biodiversity and rich cultural heritage. However, the declaration has also impacted the lives of the people in terms of what they can and cannot do, particularly to their natural resources. The project aims to explore policy options that will enhance the welfare of major stakeholders most affected by the declaration of the Batanes Protected Landscapes and Seascapes and ensure its sustainability. Specifically, it aims to examine the BPLS declaration and other related policies, and their implementation, profile the distributional effects of the Batanes protected area declaration among key stakeholders through access benefit sharing analysis, assess the policy options based on social safeguards, access and benefit-sharing, and recommend policy options that will ensure the sustainable management of BPLS and other protected areas in the Philippines. These objectives will be accomplished through the analysis of the effects of BPLS declaration and other related policies, stakeholder mapping and profiling of distributional effects, access benefit sharing analysis, multi-criteria analysis, and policy analysis. The project’s outputs will include publications in refereed journals, policy brief, audio-visual presentation, partnerships, capacitation of POs and partners, and policy

column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: The occurrence of AMR in South East Asian aquaculture has not been compiled yet and available information is still scarce. In the Philippines, few studies have been done on AMR, and a comprehensive research work on AMR in tilapia farming is non-existent at the moment. Detection of drug-resistant phenotypes and genotypes can be used to monitor and correlate bacterial infections and epidemics in different tilapia farms. Understanding disease/mortality outbreaks in tilapia aquaculture production through the lens of AMR research will help contain the spread of AMR via the aquaculture value chain and minimize their associated human health risks.

column4: Agriculture's Footprints, Gaps and Potentials Towards a Circular Bioeconomy: The Case of the Smallholder Farms in Caraga Region
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Agriculture serves an important source of livelihood and resources to Filipinos. Yet, it is not always a boon due to its environmental footprints, particularly in the Philippines as it is highly susceptible to natural disasters and climate change. It is imperative to take proactive measures to establish policies that strike a balance between economic growth and environmental sustainability, ensuring a more sustainable and resilient future for Filipinos. One promising approach to achieving this balance is through the adoption of circular bioeconomy principles, which leverages biological resources to generate value while minimizing waste and reducing negative environmental impacts. The Caraga Region, part of the fragile areas in the Philippines, faces significant challenges related to agricultural waste management. Circular bioeconomy offers a holistic approach to managing agricultural waste by turning it into valuable resources, thus closing the loop and creating a more sustainable and circular system. This project has been then initiated to assess the footprints of smallholder coconut and corn farms in the region with respect to the sustainable development goals of zero hunger and sustainable production and consumption. The project ultimately aims to develop a community-based biocircular model that can inform policymaking in the Caraga Region.

column4: Decision Support System for Effective Lake Governance of the Twin Lakes of Sibulan, Negros Oriental, Philippines
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Lakes as a natural resource are essential for their biodiversity support, freshwater supply, ecosystem services, climate regulation, role in habitat connectivity, recreation and tourism potential, and aesthetic value. Despite these, studies on lakes in the Philippines still remain few and are focused mainly on the well-known lakes. Most of these researches are concerned with the biophysical properties and biodiversity while there are hardly any studies that investigate the cross-section of human-environment interaction and governance with that of the biophysical aspect of these lakes. Furthermore, existing management plans of lakes appear to have been less effective because of inadequate consideration of human-environment interaction. Studies show that plans are unresponsive to dynamic contextual challenges and issues of the communities, which may be due to lack of reliable and updated databases. Understanding the human-environment interaction will better guide the development of management plans for lake ecosystems. This study will replicate the previous project on San Pablo lakes that is currently developing a decision support system to aid the governance of the lakes. It aims to examine the evolution of governance system and institutional arrangements in relation to the management and conservation of the Twin Lakes of Sibulan in Negros Oriental.

column4: Enhancement of captive Scylla serrata broodstock performance through optimization of light conditions and application of nanobubble oxygenation
column5: Philippine Council for Agriculture, Aquatic and Natural Resources Research and Development
column6: Mangrove crab (Scylla spp.), locally known as "alimango", is one of the most important aquaculture commodities in the Philippines. However, until recently, the farming of mangrove crabs is still dependent on wild-caught juveniles for stocking in ponds. Several crab hatcheries have been established to mitigate the lack of seedstock for farming. Recently, hatchery operators in the country have been experiencing poor larval quality and lower production that can be traced back to the broodstock quality. Hence, there is a need to fast-track the improvement of the management protocol to improve broodstock performance. In our recent project (funded by the PAARRD-DOST) using RAS with polychaete-assisted biofilter (modified RAS), initial results showed a significant improvement in the survival and spawning efficiency of S. serrata broodstock. However, more investigations need to be done to further refine the new broodstock management protocol. In this project, we aim to optimize the light intensity, spectrum, and oxygenation for the management of S. serrata broodstock using RAS. The output of this project will lead towards the development of a smart crab aquaculture technology that can reduce labor and enhance production through improved broodstock management protocol.

This 3Ps Project primarily aims to establish impact communities with different agro-ecological environments by improving their livelihood through the implementation of S&T interventions, particularly for agriculture, aquatic and natural resources. The Alangan Mangyan community in the Municipality of Victoria is one among the communities selected as initial recipients for the implementation of community-based projects. An integrated farming system will be established in Bambanin which is a two-hectare land area for the production of agricultural commodities such as banana and vegetables while aquaculture and rice production will be at Canaan. It is expected that the Theory of Change could be realized by establishing a suitable approach for an enterprise development that will generate a sustainable livelihood for them.

column6: The need for the RAISE Phase 2 initiative is underscored by the significant strides made during Phase 1 and the substantial untapped potential within the Visayas Consortium for Agriculture, Aquatic, and Natural Resources Program (ViCARP). Phase 1 successfully established foundational structures for IP management and technology commercialization. However, the full benefits remain unrealized due to persistent gaps in capacity and regional coordination. Phase 2 is critical to build upon these achievements by addressing advanced training, strategic capacity building, and robust regional networks. This phase will enhance the commercialization pathways of research outputs, driving economic growth and sustainability in the region. The continuation of the program will foster a more dynamic and responsive IP management system, ensuring innovations are protected and effectively brought to market. Additionally, Phase 2 will facilitate stronger industry-academia linkages, promoting collaborative ventures essential for technology development and diffusion. By reinforcing the regional IP and technology business framework, this phase aims to transform ViCARP into a leading hub of agricultural and natural resource innovation, significantly boosting the region's competitiveness and economic resilience. The strategic implementation of Phase 2 will ensure that ViCARP's innovations yield tangible socio-economic benefits, fostering sustainable development and regional prosperity.
