column4: Completion of the Construction of Agronomy, Soils and Horticulture Building Crop Protection Wing (UP LOS BANOS)
column6:
This construction is for the extension of the Agronomy, Soils and Horticulture Building of the UPLB College of Agriculture, a facility intended to be used by the Institute of Weed Science, Entomology and Plant Pathology in relation to teaching and research.

Entomology was the first department to be established, together with seven other departments at the College of Agriculture in 1909. It remained a purely teaching department for the first five years, with a lone teacher and an offering of two one-year courses, zoology and economic entomology, each credited for 10 units. With the offering of plant pathology in 1917, both economic entomology and plant pathology became one-semester offerings by 1918.

Through the pioneering services of American entomologists and later by Filipinos, the department gradually built up its course offerings which by 1927 included Introductory Economic Zoology, Vertebrate Zoology, Introductory Economic Ichthyology, Economic Entomology, Insect Collection and Elementary Entomology, Insects Affecting Field Crops, Insects Affecting Sugar Cane, Special Problems, Seminar, Undergraduate Thesis, and Graduate Thesis, all of which were handled by a staff of seven. By 1929, the department had produced 15 BS and 2 MS students.

The Philippines, being tropical, was a haven of a tremendous diversity of insects about which collections started to accumulate. At first the department collections were largely undetermined and were generally useless to science. With the coming of pioneer American entomologists, foremost of whom was C.F. Baker (1912-1927), an agronomist by profession but an avid insect enthusiast at heart, the collections flourished. Dr. Baker embarked on extensive collecting in the country and some parts of Borneo and accumulated the single biggest insect collection in the world from which numerous publications by foreign insect taxonomists were derived. As a result of his untiring efforts, the Philippines, especially Mt Makiling became well known in the world literature of entomology, with over 500 papers published on Philippine insects. Unfortunately, after his death in 1927, his whole collection was deposited in the U.S. National Museum, both a loss which left the department deprived of this treasure, and a blessing, because the remaining department collection was burned during the second world war.

As early as 1915-1916, the department was witness to one of the initial historic successes of biological control when some American entomologists visited Los Baños and discovered a parasitic wasp, Scolia manilae Ashmead, which when introduced to Hawaii led to the control of the white grub, Anomala orientalis Waterhouse, to the satisfaction of Hawaii sugarcane planters. As a gesture of appreciation, the Hawaiian Sugar Planters' Association donated funds for the construction of an insectary to promote entomological research in the country.

The Department of Entomology was under the tutelage of American entomologists from 1909 to 1922, and was later headed by Filipinos beginning with Dr. L.B. Uichanco (1923-1956). The department, as the College did, suffered losses and setbacks during the war (1941-1944), and began the long and tedious task of restoration in 1945. These rehabilitation efforts were enhanced by the two phases of the Cornell-Los Baños contract (1952-1969) which resulted in the improvement of facilities and courses and the academic improvement of the department faculty. 
Eventually, the College of Agriculture graduated into an autonomous University of the Philippines Los Baños in 1972, at which time the zoology courses were transferred to the department of zoology of the new College of Sciences and Humanities (now the College of Arts and Sciences).

Currently, the Institute of Weed Science, Entomology and Plant Pathology shares facilities with the Institute of Biological Sciences at the College of Arts and Sciences. Ideally, the Institute should be in close proximity with the other institutes of the College of Agriculture and Food Science with whom it shares common academic programs, research undertakings and facilities. The move to this location will make it more convenient to collaborate with other institutes. Secondly, there is a need to provide upgraded facilities and appropriate facilities to be able to attain ISO accreditation of research and analytical services as well as provide research-focused education especially for graduate students.

column4: PREEMPT, PREDICT, AND TREAT GTD (PREDICTION, EVALUATION, AND TREATMENT OF GESTATIONAL TROPHOBLASTIC DISEASES [GTD OR HMOLE AND ITS CANCER] AMONG FILIPINO WOMEN): Project 2. Predict GTN (Predictive Protein Biomarkers in Cancer Transformation to GTN)
column6: Hydatidiform mole is a type of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD) that has potential for malignant transformation (persistent trophoblastic disease or PTD) to invasive mole or choriocarcinoma. Prophylactic chemotherapy is given for at-risk groups based on identified clinical criteria, as followed by PGH, but studies have shown inconsistent results on its benefits, and the clinical factors cannot precisely identify cases that potentially become malignant. Currently, proteomic and bioinformatics technologies have been increasingly used in evaluating many diseases. It is now known that altered protein expression profiles in functional cells are associated with a number of human pathologies including malignancies. Studies on these and involving GTDs are recent and limited. Using the available tissues from cases of GTD, a study dealt with identifying potential biomarkers from proteomic profiling. The use of proteomic profiling has been used in the evaluation of diseases, including GTD. First component project of the Program aims to combine the evaluation of clinical, ultrasound and genetic parameters in identifying those cases of molar pregnancy with the risk of malignant transformation, and therefore would warrant chemoprophylaxis. The use of clinical parameters has been extensively covered in project 1. The Project 2 aims to determine potential biomarkers from blood and molar samples of women with molar pregnancy that will predict malignant transformation. This study aims to identify potential proteomic biomarkers from molar tissue and plasma among genetically confirmed molar pregnancies that can predict malignant transformation. Knowing these factors will help identify a subclass of patients that would benefit from prophylactic chemotherapy. Specific diagnostic and therapeutic targets may also be identified.

column4: PREEMPT, PREDICT, AND TREAT GTD (PREDICTION, EVALUATION, AND TREATMENT OF GESTATIONAL TROPHOBLASTIC DISEASES [GTD OR HMOLE AND ITS CANCER] AMONG FILIPINO WOMEN): Project 3. Treat GTN (Determinants of Treatment Response in GTN)
column6: In general, early diagnosis and appropriate therapy given to GTN cases will lower unnecessary cost of incorrect chemotherapeutic agents, and prevent delay in management which can result to development of high risk-metastatic disease that will require more complex management. This is a significant consideration in tertiary government centers where funds for diagnosis and therapy may be limited. Moreover, early diagnosis and appropriate therapy will avoid maternal death, while preserving the reproductive potential of these women, who will otherwise respond to chemotherapy and avoid surgery. This study aims to address these problems associated with predicting chemoresistance based on the current risk stratification and scoring systems

column4: PROGRAM TO SUPPORT THE INITIATIVES ON INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM FOR THE BETTER STATE OF HEALTH (SIBS PROGRAM): Project 2: Development of Milk Formula for Individuals with Maple Syrup Urinary Disease
column6: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is a rare inborn error of metabolism (IEM) or inherited metabolic disease (IMD) resulting from a deficiency in the enzyme branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. This deficiency causes accumulation of leucine, isoleucine and valine and their toxic byproducts (ketoacids) in the blood will result in serious health problems; irreversible neurological damage or death. Dietary management during the early stage of life also remains a challenge due to limited and expensive medical infant formula recommended for MSUD patients. All of the special or medical formulas for MSUD available in the market are imported and are expensive, hindering the recommended therapeutic intervention among low-income families. This project aims to develop medical formulas for individuals with MSUD. Local and imported raw materials will be used in the development of MSUD formula with balanced nutrition from fat, carbohydrates and protein without leucine, isoleucine and valine. Recommended vitamins and minerals for the proper growth of MSUD patients will be included in the formulation.

column4: PROGRAM TO SUPPORT THE INITIATIVES ON INBORN ERRORS OF METABOLISM FOR THE BETTER STATE OF HEALTH (SIBS PROGRAM): Project 3: Development of Recipes for Filipino Children Aged 3-10 Years Old with Maple Syrup Urine Disease
column6: Maple Syrup Urine Disease (MSUD) is an inborn error of metabolism among Filipinos that is caused by defect in the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex, which leads to an elevation in plasma branched- Page 1 of 18 DOST Form 2 DETAILED RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT PROJECT PROPOSAL (for Basic/Applied Research) chain amino acids (BCAAs). As a result, the clinical presentation includes developmental delay, growth failure, feeding difficulties, maple syrup odor in urine and death if improperly managed. Currently, there is no cure for MSUD. Management includes dietary restriction of BCAAs and close metabolic monitoring. Dietary management is challenging due to the unavailability of products that can be consumed with limited amount of BCAAs. The protein sources of MSUD patients are usually purchased abroad. To address the need to meet the nutrient requirement, the project is proposed with the aim to develop recipes that are low- protein diets to restrict the intake of BCAAs for children with MSUD. column4: Mobile Solar-Powered Grains Dryer with Advanced Electronic Heating and Iot-Based Monitoring
column6:
The Mobile Solar-Powered Grains Dryer with Advanced Electronic Heating and IoT-Based Monitoring is an applied research and development project that addresses post-harvest losses and energy inefficiencies in grain drying, particularly in island and rural agricultural communities. The project combines renewable solar energy, electronic heating control, and IoT-based monitoring to provide a mobile, efficient, and climate-resilient alternative to traditional open-sun and fuel-based drying methods.

The system integrates solar power with auxiliary electronic heating to maintain consistent drying conditions, while IoT sensors continuously monitor temperature, humidity, grain moisture, and airflow. These data are transmitted to a cloud platform and accessed through a mobile application and web dashboard, enabling real-time supervision, alerts, and data-driven decision-making by operators.

The project includes laboratory testing and field validation with farmer cooperatives, ensuring that the technology is practical, reliable, and suitable for local agricultural conditions. By improving drying efficiency and reducing dependence on fossil fuels, the project enhances grain quality, minimizes post-harvest losses, and supports sustainable agricultural practices.

Beyond technical development, the project emphasizes capacity building and technology adoption, providing training and usability evaluation to ensure accessibility for smallholder farmers and cooperatives. The resulting system is designed to be scalable and adaptable, contributing to sustainable food systems, renewable energy use, and innovation-driven agricultural development.

column4: Terrestrial and Avifauna Assessment: Understanding Diversity and Conservation Challenges in The Mangrove Forests of Surigao City, Philippines
column6:
The Terrestrial and Avifauna Assessment is an applied biodiversity research project that aims to address critical information gaps on wildlife diversity and conservation challenges in the mangrove ecosystems of Surigao City. Mangrove forests are among the most productive ecosystems, providing essential ecological services such as coastal protection, nursery grounds for marine species, and habitat for diverse terrestrial and avian fauna. However, scientific data on species composition, distribution, and conservation status within these ecosystems remain limited.

The project will conduct systematic field surveys using standard ecological methods to document amphibians, reptiles, mammals, and birds associated with mangrove habitats. Species occurrences will be assessed against international and national conservation criteria to identify threatened and endemic species. Complementary social and environmental assessments will be undertaken to identify anthropogenic pressures, existing conservation measures, and institutional challenges affecting mangrove biodiversity.

Outputs of the project include spatial distribution maps, CEPA materials, and policy briefs designed to inform local government units, environmental agencies, and community stakeholders. By translating scientific findings into actionable knowledge, the project strengthens local capacity for biodiversity conservation, sustainable land-use planning, and ecosystem-based management.

Through collaboration among higher education institutions, local government units, national agencies, and other partners, the project contributes to the protection of terrestrial ecosystems, climate resilience, and the sustainable management of coastal and mangrove environments in Surigao City.

column4: Sustainable Valorization of Fish Viscera Through Enzyme-Assisted Hydrolysis For High-Value Nutraceuticals and Functional Ingredients
column6:
The Sustainable Valorization of Fish Viscera project is an applied research initiative that addresses environmental sustainability, food innovation, and value addition in the fisheries sector by converting fish processing waste into high-value nutraceutical and functional ingredients. Fish viscera, often discarded as waste, represent a rich source of endogenous enzymes and proteins that can be harnessed through enzyme-assisted hydrolysis.

The project focuses on the extraction and characterization of enzymes from fish viscera and their application in producing protein hydrolysates with desirable functional and bioactive properties. By comparing these enzymes with commercially available alternatives, the study aims to demonstrate technical feasibility, economic viability, and environmental advantages.

The resulting hydrolysates will be evaluated for functional and bioactive properties relevant to nutraceutical, food, and functional ingredient applications. Through this approach, the project promotes circular economy principles, reduces waste from fisheries processing, and supports sustainable resource utilization.

Overall, the project strengthens research and innovation in food biotechnology, contributes to sustainable fisheries management, and supports the development of value-added products that can enhance food security, environmental protection, and innovation-driven economic growth.

The project explores the use of engineered bamboo, a renewable and low-carbon material, as a structural component for modular and foldable housing systems.

The study will evaluate the mechanical and durability properties of engineered bamboo and apply these findings to the design of housing modules that can be folded, transported, assembled, and reconfigured with minimal environmental impact. A functional prototype will be developed and subjected to structural, usability, and performance testing to ensure safety, reliability, and practicality.

By integrating modularity and foldability, the project supports flexible housing applications suitable for temporary shelters, disaster-resilient housing, and low-cost residential construction. The economic and environmental analysis will demonstrate the viability of engineered bamboo as an alternative to conventional construction materials.

The project contributes to sustainable construction practices, climate-responsive design, and innovation in housing systems, while generating technical knowledge and design guidelines that can be adopted by industry, local government units, and communities.

By improving design efficiency and passenger experience, the project supports sustainable local mobility, enhances tourism transport services, and improves income opportunities for tricycle operators. The resulting design specifications and guidelines may serve as a reference for LGUs, transport associations, and local fabricators in modernizing tricycle fleets.

column4: GIH-OMICS (Genomic Innovations for Health - Moving Towards Omics Approach): Establishment of Genomics Laboratory at DOST-V RSTL
column6:

This will also complement current research by SUCs and other line agencies towards the five priority commodities in Bicol (pili, queen pineapple, abaca, coconut, and tuber crops). Moreover, the six-year strategic plan of research consortia in Bicol incorporates the use of ‘omics technologies to promote advances in healthcare.

GIH-OMICS intends to establish a genomics laboratory at the DOST-V RSTL. This facility will expand laboratory services, promote up-to-date testing methodologies, and enhance access of Bicolano scientists/researchers. This will also complement the initiatives of SUCs, consortia, and other agencies towards improving the research in the five priority commodities in Bicol using omics-based approaches.

This project will address the demand for more sensitive and rapid testing in microbiology to enhance public health and food safety. Current research are geared towards the use of 'omics approach, enabling accurate, sensitive and rapid detection that may not be measured by the current conventional methodologies.

column4: Masbate Upcycling Center for Low-value Indigenous Fishes, Other Aquatic Resources, and their Waste Derivatives (MAS UPLIFTED)
column6: Masbate is the province in Bicol with the longest coastline and territorial waters that teem with economically valuable aquatic resources. This abundance comes with hundreds of jobs under the fisheries sector in the province, feeding families that depend on the bounty of the sea for livelihood and subsistence. The vast majority of them, however, still reel from economic and social hardships partly due to the promising economic potentials of these aquatic resources that still remain untapped. Experts estimate that as much as 70% of aquatic resources harvested from the sea end up either as low value or waste products. For example, only 40% of the fish in fillet production ends up on people's plates. The proposed project will help these fisherfolks and their families derive maximum economic benefits from the very resources they depend on by valorizing low-value fishes that are indigenous in Masbate such as sardines (lawlaw/tamban/turay) and narrow-lined puffer (buriring), and by upcycling the wastes created from processing them and other aquatic species such as scallops, squids, and crabs. The proposed project, therefore, supports a resource-efficient circular economy by creating greater value for these fishes commonly termed as "trash fish" due to their low economic value, so low that fishermen are reportedly forced to dispose of their catches, often to the detriment of the environment due to improper disposal practices. Likewise, volumes of wastes such as fish offcuts, shells, and carapace produced from processing fishery commodities remain a perennial growing concern which can otherwise be prevented by processing these wastes to create high-value products.
